slides.script:
You've just seen what Civilization Voyage feels like to play. Now I'll show you how we built it, and how we plan to turn it into a business.

This is our real working screen. We used four AI tools, and each one had one job. Lovable helped us share and test ideas. Claude handled the design. Codex built the APIs. Grok built the frontend and the 3D scenes.

With these tools, a small team can build a working game. But a working game is only the start. People need a reason to choose it, pay for it, and come back to it.

So let's start with what makes us worth choosing.

We compared ourselves with two well-known products.

Discovery Tour lets people explore detailed historical worlds, with expert-guided tours. Minecraft Education gives teachers lessons and tools across many subjects.

However, Civilization Voyage is one connected journey through Chinese and world history. The user experience will be more fluent and vivid. We have four eras, eight routes and twenty-four scenes.

That gives us three groups of customers. Players, who want a complete adventure from start to finish. Schools, where teachers look for meaningful cultural stories to bring into the classroom. And museums, which want new ways to tell their local histories.

Here is what we sell to each of them.

For players, the full game costs sixty-eight yuan. If they enjoy it, they can buy new story packs for twenty-eight yuan each. Each story pack is one new voyage. You meet two historical figures on two islands, steer through one crisis, and hear a figure on shore explain what it all meant. You keep a picture-book page of the story, and a new mark appears on your map of human ideas.

For schools, we offer a yearly package for twelve thousand yuan. It includes teaching guides, two training sessions for teachers, and support we agree on in advance. The card shows how a lesson works: students play the story, then discuss the choice they made. Each guide links the voyage to its historical sources, a lesson plan and review questions. So a teacher can run the class without designing it from scratch.

For museums, we turn a local story into a real voyage visitors can sail. A museum project costs sixty thousand yuan, and it covers three things. First, one local theme, chosen together with the museum. Second, three playable scenes, built from the museum’s own collection and research. Third, two review rounds with the museum’s experts, so the history is right. We agree on the scope before we start, and price any extra work separately.

Three customers, one engine, and in our design, each part makes the others stronger. For example, museum research becomes new story packs for players. Players show us which stories work best, and those become better lessons for schools. Classroom feedback then shows us how to explain history more clearly in the next museum project. Every project we finish improves our tools, content and process. So the more we sell, the better we get, and the less each new story costs to make.

But selling is only half the job. We also have to keep enough money after we deliver.

Now let's see what year one could look like.

In our base case, we have two thousand paying players, ten schools and two museum projects. That brings in three hundred and seventy-six thousand yuan. We spend it in two parts.

The first part goes straight back into each sale, about two hundred and fifteen thousand yuan. It pays to reach players, to train and support teachers, and to build and review each museum’s scenes. Every yuan here is tied to a sale we’ve made. That leaves around one hundred and sixty thousand.

The second part is two hundred and forty thousand yuan. It pays for developing and improving the game, researching and writing new stories, and running a small team. These are our fixed costs for the year, and every product we sell is built on them.

So in year one, our sales don't yet cover our costs. We end the year about seventy-nine thousand yuan short.

To close that gap and keep building, we're raising funding. Here's how much we need, and how we'll use it.

Our twelve-month cash plan is three hundred and sixty thousand yuan.

Two hundred and forty thousand pays for the fixed work: the game and its stories. Ninety thousand covers the gap between delivering a project and getting paid. Thirty thousand is our reserve.

But we start with one hundred and twenty thousand only. In that first stage we check one thing: do players finish a voyage and come back for new stories?

Then we work with paying schools and museums, and track the time and cost of every project. We release more money only when repeat use and paid projects show us it's working.

Every project should leave something useful for the next one: research, a teaching guide, or a better game tool. Over time, we'll have more stories to offer and less work to repeat.

And that brings me back to why we're doing this.

Every age gets a new tool. The canal. The steam engine. The telegraph cable. And now, the AI agent.

Tools change what we can do. Civilization decides what we do with them. That is why we built Civilization Voyage: to start from Chinese civilization, sail out into the world, and let every player face that choice for themselves.

That is what this business plan is for: to give civilization time. Time for good stories to be told, and time for players to think about the choices inside them.

Those choices matter in the game. They matter just as much in the world we're building today.

We can build faster ships. We still have to choose where they take us.

Let's choose a future worth arriving in. Thank you.
